title: Beacon Triage — Read the Policy Before You Touch Anything
description: beacon-only.pcapng holds four BSSs. Classify each one's security policy from the beacon itself — the answer to every task is a frame number plus the decoded field.
objectives: Decode SSID/BSSID/channel from beacons
Read RSNE AKM and RSN capability bits
Distinguish 'no RSNE' from 'RSNE with PMF'

tasks.question: How many BSSs are advertised, and on which channels?
tasks.answer: 4 BSSs: LAB-WIFI (00:11:22:33:44:55) ch6; Corp-WLAN (de:ad:be:ef:00:01) ch36; Guest-WLAN (de:ad:be:ef:00:02) ch1; LAB-OPEN (de:ad:be:ef:00:03) ch11
tasks.hint: tshark -r beacon-only.pcapng -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype == 8' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.bssid -e wlan.ssid -e wlan.ds.current_channel

tasks.question: Which BSSs advertise no RSNE at all, and what does that mean?
tasks.answer: de:ad:be:ef:00:02, de:ad:be:ef:00:03 — no RSN information element is advertised, so the beacon does not show a WPA2/WPA3 RSN policy. Check the Privacy capability and any other security IEs before distinguishing an open BSS from legacy WEP; absence alone does not establish which one it is.
tasks.hint: Filter wlan.tag.number == 48 and compare which BSSIDs appear.

tasks.question: Which BSS requires management frame protection, and which frames prove it?
tasks.answer: de:ad:be:ef:00:01 — RSN capabilities show MFPR=1 in the beacon (frame 2). MFPR is RSN capabilities bit 6 (0x0040); MFPC is bit 7 (0x0080). Advertisement is not proof of a station's negotiated PMF state.
tasks.hint: tshark -r beacon-only.pcapng -Y 'wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr == 1' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.bssid

answer_basis: computed from beacon frames with wififorge_labkit.decode
deliverable: A four-row BSS table with frame numbers and the decoded policy fields.

title: Passive Recon — Inventory, Hidden BSS and Client Leakage
description: recon-lab.pcapng is a passive capture of one site. Produce an AP/client inventory with frame numbers, then state what the capture cannot establish.
objectives: Enumerate BSSs and group them into an ESS
Show that SSID hiding leaks the name anyway
Identify client PNL leakage and MAC randomisation

tasks.question: How many BSSs and how many distinct SSIDs are present?
tasks.answer: 6 BSSs, 5 advertised SSIDs (one BSS hides its name). The two LAB-WIFI BSSIDs (00:11:22:33:44:55, 00:11:22:33:44:56) share an SSID — consistent with one ESS, but an SSID match alone does not establish membership. Correlate with an authorized inventory/controller configuration and deployment context.
tasks.hint: Count unique wlan.bssid across beacons, then unique wlan.ssid.

tasks.question: Which BSS hides its SSID, and which frame discloses it?
tasks.answer: aa:bb:cc:11:22:33 hides its SSID (SSID IE length 0 in its beacon). The probe response in frame 13 carries the SSID 'HIDDEN-LAB' in clear — which is exactly why hiding an SSID is not a security control.
tasks.hint: Filter wlan.fc.type_subtype == 5 (probe responses) and read wlan.ssid.

tasks.question: What does the client disclose, and is it trackable by MAC?
tasks.answer: Probe requests leak a preferred network list: Airport_Free_WiFi, Corp-WLAN, HIDDEN-LAB, HomeWiFi-2345, LAB-WIFI. Client addresses seen probing include 12:34:56:78:9a:bc, 22:33:44:55:66:77; 12:34:56:78:9a:bc, 22:33:44:55:66:77 use a locally administered bit (randomised MAC), so device identity is not determinable from the capture.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype == 4' -T fields -e wlan.sa -e wlan.ssid

answer_basis: computed from probe/beacon frames with wififorge_labkit.decode
deliverable: Inventory table (BSSID | SSID | ch | AKM | PMF | frames) + a limits paragraph.

title: From Capture to Evidence — One Association, Frame by Frame
description: traffic-analysis.pcapng is a deterministic one-client lifecycle fixture. Reconstruct the recorded sequence as a timeline and turn one claim into a reproducible evidence record.
objectives: Reconstruct the association state machine in order
Identify EAPOL-Key messages and their key-information flags
Package a claim with hash + filter + frames + limits

tasks.question: Give the frame sequence for the association state machine.
tasks.answer: Authentication: frame 4, frame 5; association: frame 6, frame 7; 4-way handshake (EAPOL-Key): frame 8, frame 9, frame 10, frame 11.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype == 11 || wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0 || wlan.fc.type_subtype == 1 || eapol.type == 3' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.fc.type_subtype

tasks.question: Classify every EAPOL-Key frame (M1–M4) using its key-information field.
tasks.answer: frame 8: M1 (AP → STA, ANonce, unauthenticated) (key_info=0x0088); frame 9: M2 (STA → AP, SNonce + MIC) (key_info=0x0108); frame 10: M3 (AP → STA, GTK delivery + MIC) (key_info=0x13c8); frame 11: M4 (STA → AP, MIC + Secure; final message) (key_info=0x0308). Use the flags — ACK/MIC/Install/Secure — never the order alone.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'eapol.type == 3' -T fields -e frame.number -e eapol.keydes.key_info -e eapol.keydes.replay_counter

tasks.question: What EAPOL-Key sequence is recorded, and what additional evidence would be needed to claim a real client completed a WPA2 handshake with a production BSS?
tasks.answer: Artefact: traffic-analysis.pcapng (SHA-256 in MANIFEST.md); filter: eapol.type == 3; frames: 8/9/10/11; interpretation: the fixture contains an M1→M4 sequence with replay counters and MICs that verify against its documented lab PMK. Limit: this synthetic capture does not establish RF delivery, AP acceptance, or a production client/session. A live claim needs authorized capture plus client/AP logs and association context; user identity is not established by the shared PSK.
tasks.hint: Hash + filter + frame numbers + interpretation + limit. A claim without all five is an opinion.

answer_basis: computed from EAPOL/management frames with wififorge_labkit.decode
deliverable: A frame-numbered timeline plus one complete evidence record.

title: Two Clients, One Complete Handshake
description: wpa2-handshake.pcapng has a complete M1–M4 exchange and a truncated M1–M2. Decide what each one is worth for an offline audit, and verify the MIC yourself.
objectives: Identify M1–M4 from key_info flags
Explain why M1+M2 is enough for an offline audit
Re-derive a MIC from the documented lab PSK

tasks.question: Which frames are M1–M4, and for which client?
tasks.answer: M1: frame 6, frame 12; M2: frame 7, frame 13; M3: frame 8; M4: frame 9. The complete exchange belongs to 12:34:56:78:9a:bc; the second client has M1/M2 recorded but no M3/M4 in this capture; that absence does not establish what the station actually received.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'eapol.type == 3' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.sa -e eapol.keydes.key_info

tasks.question: Why is the truncated exchange still usable for an offline audit?
tasks.answer: M2 carries the MIC computed with the KCK, and the KCK is derived from the PMK — so a candidate passphrase can be tested entirely offline. M3/M4 add GTK delivery and confirmation, not crackability. The missing M3/M4 in this capture may reflect capture loss or a partial exchange; it does not by itself prove an availability/interoperability failure. The M1/M2 material remains auditable.
tasks.hint: Ask which message lets an attacker verify a candidate key.

tasks.question: Reproduce the audit end to end (documented lab PSK).
tasks.answer: PMK = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1('ForgeLab2026!', 'LAB-WIFI', 4096, 256) = 5e6c57194b8b7e08f998055eade832d4…; the MICs in the capture verify against this PMK (scripts/verify-lab-artifacts.py performs the KCK→MIC check). In hashcat terms: hcxpcapngtool -o audit.hc22000 wpa2-handshake.pcapng, then hashcat -m 22000 audit.hc22000 wordlists/wififorge-lab-psk.txt --show.
tasks.hint: PMK → PTK (PRF-512 over both MACs and nonces) → KCK → HMAC-SHA1 over the EAPOL-Key frame with the MIC zeroed.

answer_basis: computed from EAPOL-Key frames; MIC verification in scripts/verify-lab-artifacts.py
deliverable: A short audit note: frames, PMK derivation, hashcat result, and what the key grants.

title: PMKID Without a Full Handshake — The KDE in M1
description: pmkid.pcapng holds a single EAPOL-Key M1 with a PMKID key data encapsulation. Decide why this matters operationally and what it does not prove.
objectives: Locate the PMKID KDE inside M1 key data
Reproduce the PMKID from the PSK
Compare PMKID collection without a full handshake with a 4-way capture

tasks.question: Where is the PMKID, and what is its value?
tasks.answer: frame 6: M1 key data is 'dd14000fac04' + the 16-byte PMKID = 21cec8aea8409d8ce49ae29d4e4a28ee (KDE: element 221, length 20, OUI 00-0F-AC, type 04).
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'eapol.type == 3' -T fields -e frame.number -e eapol.keydes.key_data

tasks.question: Verify the PMKID from the documented lab PSK and the BSSID/client addresses.
tasks.answer: PMKID = HMAC-SHA1-128(PMK, 'PMK Name' | AA | SPA) with AA=00:11:22:33:44:55 and SPA=44:55:66:77:88:99 reproduces 21cec8aea8409d8ce49ae29d4e4a28ee, where PMK = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1('ForgeLab2026!', 'LAB-WIFI', 4096, 256). That is why a PMKID is crackable material: it is a keyed hash of the PMK.
tasks.hint: python3 -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'scripts');from wififorge_labkit import *" — or read scripts/verify-lab-artifacts.py.

tasks.question: What is the operational difference from a 4-way handshake capture?
tasks.answer: A PMKID-bearing M1 can provide offline-verification material without capturing all four EAPOL-Key messages, and may be collected passively without deauthentication when an AP emits it for an associated client. It is not necessarily clientless: an association/exchange must occur and AP behavior varies. The material permits offline PSK guesses; a missing PMKID proves nothing about passphrase strength.
tasks.hint: Think about what you would otherwise have to do to a live client.

answer_basis: PMKID read from the capture and recomputed with wififorge_labkit.pmkid
deliverable: PMKID value + derivation + a note on collection trade-offs.

title: WPS State — Configuration Exposure vs Exploitability
description: wps-beacon.pcapng advertises WPS on two BSSs with different states. Decide what can and cannot be concluded, and write the finding without over-claiming.
objectives: Decode WPS IE attributes
Separate a configuration finding from a demonstrated exploit
Write remediation and retest criteria

tasks.question: Which BSS advertises Setup Locked, and what WPS methods/registrar state are visible on each?
tasks.answer: Setup Locked not advertised: ff:00:11:22:33:44; Setup Locked set: ff:00:11:22:33:45 (frame 1, frame 2 carry the WPS IE). Decoded WPS state: ff:00:11:22:33:44: PIN/label, display, push-button; setup_locked=False; selected_registrar=True; ff:00:11:22:33:45: PIN/label, push-button; setup_locked=True; selected_registrar=False. These beacon fields do not prove live reachability, successful enrollment, or lockout behavior.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'wlan.tag.number == 221' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.bssid -e wps.ap_setup_locked -e wps.config_methods

tasks.question: Is 'WPS enabled with the PIN method' exploitable on its own?
tasks.answer: No — it is a configuration exposure. Exploitability also requires: the PIN registrar to be reachable, no effective lockout (the 8-digit PIN is ~11 000 guesses because the last digit is a checksum and the halves are validated separately), and an authorised window to attempt it. In this capture no PIN attack was performed, so the finding is stated as exposure with the attack left as a testable condition.
tasks.hint: Compare the two states and ask what evidence you would need for each claim.

tasks.question: State the remediation and how you would retest it.
tasks.answer: Disable WPS entirely (hostapd: wps_state=0) — the only complete fix for the PIN method. Where a product requires WPS, enforce lockout and use PBC with a monitored window. Retest: re-enumerate the BSS and show the WPS IE is gone (or setup-locked with enforced lockout verified by a controlled attempt), then attempt one WSC exchange and record the rejection.
tasks.hint: Remediation + verification, not just 'disable WPS'.

answer_basis: WPS attributes decoded from beacons in the capture
deliverable: A configuration finding (not an exploit claim) with retest criteria.

title: WPA3-Only — Proving a Control Holds
description: wpa3-only.pcapng is a synthetic teaching fixture advertising SAE-only policy. State what its frames show, what they do not validate, and how to write a bounded no-finding conclusion.
objectives: Read AKM and PMF from the RSNE
Explain why SAE resists offline guessing
Write a 'no finding' section that a reviewer can trust

tasks.question: Classify the deployment from the RSNE.
tasks.answer: ee:ff:00:11:22:34: LAB-WPA3 — AKM SAE (WPA3-Personal), MFPC=1, MFPR=1. WPA3-Personal only: no PSK AKM, so there is no 4-way handshake with crackable material in the capture.
tasks.hint: Filter wlan.tag.number == 48 -e wlan.rsn.akms.type -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpc -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr

tasks.question: Why can't the SAE exchange be turned into an offline audit?
tasks.answer: SAE (Dragonfly) derives the session key from a password-authenticated key exchange: neither commit nor confirm exposes a keyed verification value that lets a candidate password be tested offline from a passive transcript alone when correctly implemented; implementation flaws and side channels remain possible. A guess generally requires a live exchange, but rate limiting is implementation-dependent. SAE is designed to provide forward secrecy when ephemeral values are generated and handled correctly. The abbreviated synthetic frames in this fixture do not validate a real SAE exchange.
tasks.hint: Contrast with the MIC in M2 of a PSK handshake.

tasks.question: What does the protected deauthentication frame prove?
tasks.answer: frame 6: the fixture marks this deauthentication frame protected and includes a BIP MIC-like field. The capture's IGTK is synthetic/unknown, so it does not prove the MIC is cryptographically valid or that a receiver accepted the frame. The beacon's MFPR advertisement is direct policy evidence; validate PMF behavior using an authorized client/AP test.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype == 12' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.fc.protected

answer_basis: RSNE/PMF fields decoded from the capture
deliverable: A documented negative result: tests performed, evidence, limits.

title: Transition Mode — Evidence of a PSK Association
description: wpa3-transition.pcapng shows a BSS advertising both PSK and SAE, plus a captured PSK handshake. Document which path the fixture shows; it does not prove that an attacker induced a downgrade.
objectives: Identify a mixed AKM list
Identify the captured PSK association without claiming it was attacker-induced
Word the finding without claiming 'WPA3 is broken'

tasks.question: What policy does the BSS advertise?
tasks.answer: ee:ff:00:11:22:33: LAB-WPA3-TRANS — advertised AKMs PSK, SAE (WPA3-Personal); MFPC=1, MFPR=0. In this fixture PSK and SAE are both advertised, with PMF capable (MFPC=1) but not required (MFPR=0). This does not establish what a deployed client negotiated.
tasks.hint: Read wlan.rsn.akms.type — a list with two entries means transition mode.

tasks.question: Which station's recorded association trace uses PSK rather than SAE, and what evidence supports that reading?
tasks.answer: SAE-shaped authentication frames (algorithm 3) involve station 22:33:44:55:66:77: frame 2, frame 3, frame 4, frame 5. The station 12:34:56:78:9a:bc has open-system authentication (algorithm 0) at frame 6, frame 7 followed by EAPOL-Key frames frame 8, frame 9, frame 10, frame 11 — evidence of a PSK handshake against a BSS that also advertises SAE. The synthetic SAE payloads do not prove a valid SAE exchange, and the PSK path does not prove an attacker induced a downgrade.
tasks.hint: Client MACs differ between the two flows; correlate the authentication algorithm with the following handshake.

tasks.question: Write the finding: one sentence of claim plus remediation.
tasks.answer: Claim: the beacon advertises PSK as well as SAE and the fixture contains a PSK handshake; it does not show an induced downgrade or establish a weak production passphrase. If PSK compatibility is unnecessary, consider SAE-only with PMF required; otherwise assess passphrase strength and client negotiation in an authorized deployment test.
tasks.hint: Scope the claim to the captured PSK association; do not assert that an attacker induced a downgrade.

answer_basis: authentication algorithms and EAPOL-Key frames decoded from the capture
deliverable: A scoped finding plus remediation/exception plan.

title: Availability Testing — Frames, Effect and Reason Codes
description: deauth.pcapng is a synthetic frame sequence with broadcast/directed deauthentication and disassociation, two SA Query-shaped action frames, and BSSs advertising different PMF capabilities. Frames alone do not prove delivery, acceptance, or service impact.
objectives: Interpret reason codes as evidence
Explain why PMF changes the outcome
State the evidence an availability finding requires

tasks.question: Summarise the deauthentication traffic: how many frames, which reasons, broadcast or directed?
tasks.answer: reason codes present: [1, 7, 8, 15]; broadcast deauthentication set: 12 frames (frame 3, frame 4, frame 5, frame 6…); directed frames: 5 (frame 15, frame 16, frame 18, frame 19, frame 20). Reason 1 = unspecified (not attribution or proof of tooling), 7 = class-3 frame from a nonassociated station, 8 = STA leaving, 15 = 4-way handshake timeout.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype == 12' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.fixed.reason_code -e wlan.da

tasks.question: Which BSS advertises PMF required, and what SA Query-shaped traffic is present in the fixture?
tasks.answer: aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:fe advertises MFPR=1. Frames frame 21, frame 22 carry category-8 SA Query-shaped request/response bytes in this synthetic fixture. They do not prove a valid protected exchange, PTK possession, or that a real client rejected a deauthentication.
tasks.hint: Filter wlan.fc.type_subtype == 13 and look at the action category.

tasks.question: What evidence would you need before reporting an availability finding?
tasks.answer: Transmission plus effect plus timing: the deauth frames, a client-side disconnection record (supplicant log or AP logs) and the re-association timeline, all on one clock reference — and an impact statement naming the population and duration. A packet record alone does not prove that a real frame was transmitted/delivered or that clients were removed.
tasks.hint: Caution: 'we sent 200 deauths' is not an impact statement.

answer_basis: deauthentication/action frames decoded from the capture
deliverable: An availability finding with effect evidence or an explicit statement that effect was not tested.

title: Rogue Infrastructure — Build the Case From Signals
description: rogue-ap.pcapng contains an enterprise-style BSS and a same-SSID look-alike with differing advertised settings. No authorized BSSID inventory is supplied; decide what the capture supports and what remains unproven.
objectives: Compare BSSID administration bits, RSNE and beacon parameters
Reconstruct the frame order and distinguish sequence from causation
Separate rogue-AP risk from client-impersonation risk

tasks.question: Which BSS is the look-alike? What additional evidence is needed before calling it unauthorized?
tasks.answer: 02:11:22:33:44:55: locally administered MAC (bit 1 of the first octet set: True), different AKM (PSK) from the other captured BSS de:ad:be:ef:00:01 (802.1X (EAP)), different IE fingerprint and channel plan. No single signal is proof — the case is the combination, ideally corroborated by the authorised inventory.
tasks.hint: Compare wlan.bssid, wlan.rsn.akms.type and wlan.fixed.beacon for both BSSIDs.

tasks.question: Reconstruct what happened to the client, with frames.
tasks.answer: The fixture records deauthentication frame(s) frame 3, frame 4, a probe request frame 5, then a probe response/association with the look-alike (frame 6, frame 9) and a 4-way handshake (frame 11, frame 12, frame 13, frame 14). The documented weak lab PSK (password123) reproduces the handshake MIC; the sequence does not prove the deauth reached the client or caused association. No encrypted client payload traffic is included; the handshake could support offline audit/decryption of separately captured traffic.
tasks.hint: Order the frames you already have; the sequence is the evidence.

tasks.question: Write a bounded finding or no-finding conclusion for the look-alike and client association. What evidence would establish unauthorized ownership and real client impact?
tasks.answer: The capture shows a same-SSID look-alike with different advertised security/IEs and a client association/handshake sequence, but it does not establish unauthorized ownership, a real client profile, or that an attack caused the association. Compare against an authorized BSSID/IE inventory and correlate wired-side ownership/logs before calling it a rogue. In a controlled client test, verify profile/AKM behavior and impact. Controls may include managed enterprise certificate validation, appropriate WPA3/PMF policy, WIDS with an authorized baseline, and a documented response; do not infer credential capture or rotate credentials without evidence.
tasks.hint: Different impacts, different owners, different controls.

answer_basis: beacon/EAPOL frames decoded from the capture
deliverable: A bounded finding or no-finding conclusion, with additional evidence and safe tests needed to establish ownership/impact.

title: Guest Portal and Client Isolation
description: captive-portal.pcapng is a packet-level open-network simulation with an HTTP portal flow and a two-station ARP exchange. Distinguish fixture evidence from claims that would require a real service or network test.
objectives: Trace the HTTP flow and identify bytes visible in the fixture
Test isolation and segmentation claims separately
Write findings at the level the evidence supports

tasks.question: Reconstruct the portal flow and identify which values are visible in plaintext in this fixture.
tasks.answer: Open association → DHCP DORA → HTTP connectivity-check GET → 302 redirect → cleartext POST with lab-only values → HTTP response with Set-Cookie. The fixture exposes those bytes on an open BSS, but it does not implement a real portal, prove that a server trusts the MAC in the URL, or demonstrate session hijacking; those require controlled service-side tests and logs.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e frame.number -e http.request.method -e http.host -e http.request.uri

tasks.question: Does the capture show client isolation? Which frames decide it?
tasks.answer: The synthetic packet sequence shows an ARP request from 12:34:56:78:9a:bc forwarded by the AP to 55:66:77:88:99:aa, followed by the peer reply forwarded back. That demonstrates the fixture models station-to-station forwarding; it does not establish a real AP setting or production isolation failure. The capture says nothing about guest-to-corporate segmentation, which needs a separate scoped test.
tasks.hint: Look for ARP between two non-AP MACs.

tasks.question: Prioritise the remediation and justify the order.
tasks.answer: Prioritize TLS/HTTPS for the portal and server-side session controls, then validate guest client isolation and inter-VLAN policy independently. The fixture demonstrates cleartext HTTP bytes and simulated peer ARP forwarding only; it does not establish a MAC-based authorization flaw or prove an actual production control is absent.
tasks.hint: Rank by what an attacker gains and how easily.

answer_basis: HTTP/ARP frames decoded from the capture
deliverable: Two bounded fixture observations (visible HTTP values and modeled station-to-station forwarding) plus separate authorized portal/isolation/segmentation test plans.

title: 802.1X Path — From EAPOL-Start to Keys
description: enterprise.pcapng is an abbreviated synthetic EAPOL/EAP teaching fixture. Reconstruct the visible frames, then distinguish protocol concepts from what this capture cannot prove: no complete TLS/PEAP session, RADIUS exchange or deployed policy is bundled.
objectives: Map supplicant → authenticator → RADIUS → identity store
Explain the MSK→PMK→PTK relationship
Decide what a passive capture can and cannot show

tasks.question: List the EAP methods and the order of the exchange.
tasks.answer: EAP type labels present in the fixture: Identity, PEAP. Visible frame order includes EAPOL/EAP identifiers and EAPOL-Key frames (frame 8, frame 9, frame 10, frame 11). TLS bytes are abbreviated structural data and the MSK is inserted lab data; this does not prove a complete PEAP tunnel, real inner identity, or successful production authentication.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'eap' -T fields -e frame.number -e eap.code -e eap.type

tasks.question: Why is there still a 4-way handshake after successful EAP authentication?
tasks.answer: EAP produces the MSK; the PMK is the first 256 bits of it (per user, per session). The 4-way handshake then proves both sides hold the PMK, derives the PTK (KCK/KEK/TK) bound to the MAC addresses and nonces, and installs keys including the GTK. If no handshake appears in a capture, the capture alone cannot distinguish an incomplete recording from a failed/aborted exchange; consult client/AP logs and session context.
tasks.hint: The two exchanges derive different keys for different purposes.

tasks.question: What can a passive capture of this flow prove about credential exposure?
tasks.answer: This fixture cannot establish credential exposure or the client's certificate-validation behavior. Its TLS bytes are structural and the MSK is inserted; it does not contain a complete TLS tunnel or a validated client authentication. In a real PEAP test, a client profile that fails to validate both a trusted CA and expected server identity can be vulnerable to a rogue authenticator; that requires an authorized, scoped test.
tasks.hint: State the precondition for the attack rather than assuming the capture demonstrates it.

answer_basis: EAP/EAPOL frames decoded from the capture
deliverable: A role-labelled flow diagram plus a precondition analysis.

title: EAP Methods and MS-CHAPv2 Material
description: eap.pcapng contains abbreviated EAP method identifiers and an intentionally direct MS-CHAPv2 teaching exchange. It is not a set of complete PEAP, EAP-TLS or EAP-TTLS sessions; analyse the visible fields and state what the fixture cannot prove.
objectives: Identify methods from outer exchanges
Extract and verify MS-CHAPv2 material
Explain the certificate-validation precondition

tasks.question: Which EAP methods appear, and what does each protect?
tasks.answer: The fixture contains EAP type identifiers for PEAP (25), EAP-TLS (13), EAP-TTLS (21) and direct EAP-MSCHAPv2 (26) packets. These are abbreviated method examples, not complete TLS sessions or proof that MS-CHAPv2 occurred inside PEAP/TTLS. In general, PEAP/TTLS rely on client validation of the server certificate; EAP-TLS uses client certificates and does not authenticate with a password.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y 'eap.type == 25 || eap.type == 13 || eap.type == 21 || eap.type == 26'

tasks.question: Extract the MS-CHAPv2 challenge/response pair and say what makes it crackable.
tasks.answer: Challenge frames frame 10 and Response frames frame 11: the fixture's response contains the peer challenge, NT-Response and username. This is deliberately direct, visible EAP-MSCHAPv2 material—not evidence that a PEAP tunnel was terminated. The NT-Response construction permits offline password guesses; scripts/verify-lab-artifacts.py verifies the fixture against the documented lab password and RFC 2759 vector.
tasks.hint: In this fixture the direct MS-CHAPv2 packets are intentionally exposed; do not infer a tunnel from an EAP type label.

tasks.question: State the precondition and the controls that remove it.
tasks.answer: Precondition: a compatible client accepts an untrusted/wrong-identity server and an authorized rogue authenticator successfully negotiates the tunneled method; missing validation alone does not prove credential capture. Controls include EAP-TLS with managed client certificates; enforce the intended CA and expected server name in every profile; disable PEAP-MSCHAPv2 server-side where possible; use PMF to reduce spoofed deauth/disassoc paths (not as AP authentication); monitor look-alike BSSIDs against an authorized baseline.
tasks.hint: Controls belong at the client profile, the RADIUS policy and the radio.

answer_basis: EAP/MS-CHAPv2 fields decoded from the capture; RFC 2759 derivation checked in verify-lab-artifacts.py
deliverable: A precondition analysis plus a layered remediation.

title: RADIUS — Verifiable Integrity and Trust Boundaries
description: radius.pcapng contains an authentication exchange, an accounting pair, a rogue NAS request and policy attributes. Verify the integrity fields yourself before drawing conclusions.
objectives: Read codes and attributes as evidence
Verify Message-Authenticator and Response Authenticator
Assess the shared secret as a high-value credential

tasks.question: List the RADIUS packets with codes and the EAP method inside them.
tasks.answer: frame 2: Access-Request / Identity; frame 3: Access-Challenge / PEAP; frame 4: Access-Request / MS-CHAPv2; frame 5: Access-Challenge / MS-CHAPv2; frame 6: Access-Accept / MS-CHAPv2; frame 7: Access-Request; frame 8: Accounting-Response; frame 9: Access-Request / Identity. Note EAP-Message can be split across several attributes: concatenate every type-79 attribute before parsing, or the EAP packet will be silently truncated.
tasks.hint: tshark -Y radius -T fields -e frame.number -e radius.code -e radius.eap_message

tasks.question: Verify integrity: what does the Message-Authenticator prove, and why does one request fail?
tasks.answer: Message-Authenticator = HMAC-MD5 over the packet with the attribute value zeroed, keyed with the shared secret — a valid value supports integrity under that shared secret, but does not uniquely identify which holder sent the packet. Recomputing it for each request with the documented lab secret verifies the exchange; the rogue-NAS request in the capture was built with a different secret and fails verification, which is exactly what you should reproduce by hand. Responses additionally carry the Response Authenticator (MD5 over code|id|length|request authenticator|attributes|secret).
tasks.hint: Zero the 16-byte attribute value before hashing, then compare with the captured value.

tasks.question: What is the impact of a leaked shared secret, and what limits it?
tasks.answer: A party holding the secret can validate/construct packets for that shared-secret relationship and recover User-Password attributes from captured requests; impersonation also depends on network reachability and server/NAS policy. Source-IP allowlists, unique per-device secrets, protected RadSec peers and prompt rotation reduce exposure, but none makes a leaked secret harmless. The fixture demonstrates verification under its lab secret, not production compromise.
tasks.hint: Environmental preconditions decide severity — test them, do not assume them.

answer_basis: RADIUS attributes and authenticators decoded/verified from the capture
deliverable: A verification record (packet bytes, secret used, calculation) plus an impact analysis.

Choose tests by expected impact, not by tool availability

tasks.question: Prioritise the test sequence and justify it.
tasks.answer: Start with passive inventory and decode beacon/RSNE/WPS fields. Next, audit only the supplied weak-PSK practice handshake offline. Treat the open Guest beacon as a policy observation—not proof of portal behavior or exposed user traffic. The look-alike and EAP/MS-CHAPv2 frames are synthetic examples; ownership, a complete PEAP flow, certificate validation, or credential capture require authorized inventory/profile review and controlled tests. Test availability and segmentation only with explicit scope, named clients, controls and impact monitoring.
tasks.hint: Cheapest, least disruptive, highest information first.

tasks.question: Write the finding list with severity reasoning and retest criteria.
tasks.answer: Evidence-bounded report: (a) the supplied LAB-WEAK-PSK fixture contains a handshake for the documented weak training passphrase—this is not a production credential; retest a real scoped SSID after rotation. (b) Guest-WLAN advertises no RSNE in its beacon—this does not prove portal behavior, client-to-client access or cleartext credentials; inspect the actual portal and controlled traffic. (c) WPS information elements appear in beacons—this does not prove a PIN attack is possible; inspect setup lock/rate limiting and test only with authorization. (d) a look-alike BSSID, abbreviated EAP/MS-CHAPv2 fields, one deauth and an ICMP pair are present, but these do not establish a rogue owner, completed PEAP credential capture, client disconnection or production segmentation. For each, state the evidence, limitation, impact assumption, and a concrete authorized retest; assign severity only after scope and likelihood/impact are known.
tasks.hint: Four findings, four retests, each stating what would falsify it.
